title: Grace
lead: Grace is God's favor and kindness, freely given. The Greek charis and the Hebrew chen both mean favor or kindness that is given, not earned; Christian traditions differ on how grace works in a person.

sections.h: Grace in the Old and New Testaments
sections.b: "Noah found favor in the LORD's eyes" (Genesis 6:8); the word for favor is chen. God reveals himself as "compassionate and gracious" (Exodus 34:6). In the New Testament grace becomes a summary of the gospel: "by grace you have been saved through faith... it is the gift of God" (Ephesians 2:8–9); "the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation" (Titus 2:11).
sections.refs: Genesis 6:8; Exodus 34:6; John 1:14–17; Romans 3:24; Ephesians 2:8–9; Titus 2:11–12

sections.b: From the start, some heard "grace" as permission to sin. Paul answers, "Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase? Certainly not!" (Romans 6:1–2). Titus 2:11–12 says grace itself teaches us to turn away from ungodliness. The debate over antinomianism (from Greek anti, "against," and nomos, "law") runs through church history.

Protestant teaching stresses grace as God's undeserved favor: God accepts sinners freely, for Christ's sake, received by faith (Ephesians 2:8–9). Catholic teaching also speaks of grace as a participation in God's own life, poured into the soul, that heals and transforms (Catechism of the Catholic Church 1996–1999). Orthodox teaching speaks of grace as God's own energies, drawing believers into theosis, becoming "partakers of the divine nature" (2 Peter 1:4). In Jewish thought, God's chen and chesed are shown within the covenant, and keeping the Torah is a response to God's prior kindness, not a way to earn it.
